narrative:
The model estimated a 68% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is a risk signal above the threshold the review process treated as too high, so your law-school application was denied rather than being judged on a guarantee about your future. The assessment did not use your gender or race.

The denial was driven most strongly by your year-three class standing. Your year-three decile of 1 was far below the accepted students’ average near 5.8, and this was the single most influential factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 18, compared with an accepted-student average of about 37.2; this also pushed strongly toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20, against an accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor, but it worked in your favor by slightly reducing the predicted failure risk. It was simply not enough to offset the two stronger concerns.

To improve your position, focus on the areas the review identified. Prepare for and retake the LSAT if feasible, and strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program that demonstrates readiness for law study. Seek admissions advising about how to explain any context behind your year-three grades, consider law-related work or internships, and reapply after meaningful improvement or to programs that review applicants more holistically. If you are admitted elsewhere, start bar-exam preparation early.
